title: Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde
summary: Cliff Palace, in a sandstone alcove at Mesa Verde in south-west Colorado, is the largest cliff dwelling in North America, with about 150 rooms and 23 kivas. Ancestral Pueblo people built it between about AD 1190 and 1280, most of it in the last twenty years, and left it in the 13th century.

uncertainty.note: The National Park Service gives construction as ongoing from AD 1190 to AD 1280, with the main phase 1260-1280; tree-ring dates run from 1190-1191 to at least 1280. End is the present: the ruin stands.

when.display: Built c. AD 1190–1280; abandoned in the 13th century

importance.justification: The largest cliff dwelling in North America and the best-known monument of the Ancestral Pueblo world, within a UNESCO World Heritage park.

footprint.description: A long curved row of room blocks, plazas and towers filling an alcove about 215 feet wide and 90 feet deep, with the dwelling itself about 300 feet long (NPS 1920). No surveyed footprint is stored; register figures only.

phases.description: Tree-ring dates show building from AD 1190-1191 and from 1209 through at least 1280; the main phase was 1260-1280.
Unpeopled since the thirteenth century; the Wetherills found it in December 1888. The start year is the end of dated construction, not a documented departure.
Jesse Walter Fewkes excavated the alcove and repaired the crumbling walls in 1909.
